clue.text: Frenzied demoniac - scream!

indicators.note: Somebody frenzied is beyond control and does nothing in the proper order, so the letters beside the word are not to be read in the order given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Someone in a demonic frenzy letting out a shriek.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes the last word look like the end of the picture rather than a definition standing on its own. A scream here is a person, not a noise: 'she's an absolute scream' is British for very funny indeed.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling somebody a scream is the British way of saying they are hilarious, which is what a comedian is paid to be.

clue.text: Recording equipment, love, in which you won't be seen

definitions.text: in which you won't be seen
definitions.note: The definition describes the answer instead of naming it, which is fair because camo is defined by its one purpose: whoever wears it is not picked out.

blocks.note: a cam is a camera, the short form that gives us dashcam and webcam
love is nothing in tennis scoring, written as a nought

explanation.surface: Filming gear offered to a sweetheart as somewhere they will never be spotted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' sits between two commas exactly where an endearment would, and it is the tennis nought. Both pieces are short forms, which is fitting for an answer that is itself short for camouflage.
explanation.definitionFit: Camo is camouflage clothing, worn so that the wearer cannot be told apart from the background behind them.

clue.text: June maybe taking heart in winged creature

indicators.note: To take the heart out of a word is to lift away the letter at its centre, leaving the two halves to close up.

blocks.note: June is one of the twelve months, and 'maybe' asks for the general word rather than the example

explanation.surface: A woman called June drawing courage from a passing insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking heart' is encouragement on the surface and surgery underneath. The capital J invites you to see a person, and the wordplay needs June read as one of the twelve.
explanation.definitionFit: A moth is an insect with wings, flying at night where its cousin the butterfly flies by day.

clue.text: Upset? Shave?

blocks.note: read as the plain verb: to trouble somebody, to put them in a state
read as an instruction rather than a word: a tress is a lock of hair, and the three letters in front of it are the prefix that undoes what follows

explanation.surface: A barber's two brisk questions to a customer in a bad mood.
explanation.walkthrough: The question marks are the setter owning up to the second reading, which no dictionary carries: split after the first three letters and the word promises the removal of hair. Both halves are verbs, which is what lets them sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To distress somebody is to upset them; and read as dis-tress, a tress being a lock of hair, the same letters promise the removal a shave carries out.

clue.text: Once more, a win

blocks.note: the article is taken exactly as it stands
the ground a side takes in a match is its gain, and to win ground is to gain it

explanation.surface: Chalking up one more victory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A win' reads as one idea and is two pieces, the article kept as written and the noun swapped for a synonym. Both words of the definition are needed: 'once' alone would not do it.
explanation.definitionFit: Again means one more time, so 'once more' says the same thing in two words.

clue.text: Part of Pacific Rim, Eastern Peninsula

indicators.note: A part of a thing is a piece of it taken as it stands, so the letters lie unbroken and in order in the words that follow.

blocks.note: six consecutive letters starting on the last letter of Pacific and running across both the space and the comma

explanation.surface: A stretch of the Pacific Rim lying away to the east.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital letters on 'Rim' and 'Eastern' make the words look like the name of a region, and that is what keeps the run out of sight. Crimea is the diamond of land hanging off southern Ukraine into the Black Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Crimea is joined to the mainland by one narrow isthmus and surrounded by sea on every other side, which is what makes it a peninsula.

clue.text: Regretting being in Peru, in general

indicators.note: To be in something is to sit inside it, so the letters wanted are already lying within the words that follow.

blocks.note: five consecutive letters starting two letters into Peru, crossing the comma and swallowing the whole of 'in'

explanation.surface: Having second thoughts about a stay in Peru, broadly speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In general' reads as a qualifier on the whole remark and is holding three of the five letters. A comma dropped inside a hidden run is the best cover a setter has.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue a thing is to regret it, a verb that survives mostly in 'rue the day'.

clue.text: Roman currency of old given to worker only (not 'pounds')

indicators.note: Not rules a thing out, so whatever it names is struck out of the letters standing beside it.

blocks.note: the mark was Germany's money until the euro replaced it
the ant is the crossword's standard worker, the insect that never stops
ONLY with its L lifted out
pounds is L, the abbreviation still printed on the £ sign, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: An old coin handed to a labourer who will take payment in anything but sterling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worker' is the ant every time, and the bracket at the end is an instruction rather than an aside. Mark Antony was Caesar's lieutenant, the one Shakespeare hands the funeral speech to.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Antony was a Roman general and consul, so the bare word names him once the wordplay has settled which Roman is meant.

clue.text: A familiar query, regularly seen: Everyman, quiet and unprofessional?

indicators.note: What is seen regularly turns up at even intervals, so every other letter of the word is taken and the rest left behind.

blocks.note: the article stands as itself
a familiar is somebody you know well, which is a mate
the second and fourth letters of QUERY, taken at every second step
the setter signs himself Everyman, so when he appears in his own clue he is the first person
sh is the noise made at somebody to ask for quiet

explanation.surface: Wondering aloud whether the crossword setter keeps quiet because he is not much good at it.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman writes himself into a clue most weeks, and the letter he hands over is I. Five pieces in ten letters is what makes this hard: 'query' surrenders only two of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Amateurish work is done with an amateur's clumsiness, which is what calling it unprofessional accuses it of.

clue.text: Mum with pen, perhaps one that glides across water

blocks.note: keeping mum is keeping silent, which is what mute means
a pen is a female swan, so 'perhaps' asks for the bird in general rather than the particular name

explanation.surface: A silent mother sitting with a pen in her hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum with pen' is a mother writing a letter, and neither word means what it looks like. The male of the bird is a cob and the young are cygnets; only the female is a pen.
explanation.definitionFit: The mute swan is the big white swan of British rivers and park lakes, and gliding is exactly how it crosses the water.

clue.text: In report, recognise clotheshorse and range

indicators.note: A report is what somebody is heard to say, so what counts is the sound of the words and not the way they are spelt.

blocks.note: to recognise a thing is to see it, and a clotheshorse is an airer, the folding frame British homes dry washing on; the two said together make the answer

explanation.surface: A news report in which a clothes rack and a cooking range are both identified.
explanation.walkthrough: Two flat English words said one after another turn into a Spanish mountain name, which is why the join has to be heard rather than read. 'Range' looks like part of the kitchen on the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A sierra is a range of mountains, the jagged sort named from the Spanish for a saw.

clue.text: Most pleasant rue on the Riviera

blocks.note: Nice is the principal city of the French Riviera
rue is French for street, printed in italics to mark it as the foreign word, and street shortens to ST

explanation.surface: The loveliest street to be found anywhere along the French Riviera.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics mark the three-letter word as French rather than the English verb for regret. A rue on the Riviera is a street in Nice, and written out as an address that is the town and then the ST.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicest is the superlative of nice, matching 'most pleasant' in sense and in degree.

clue.text: Contest in which losers are roaring?

definitions.text: Contest in which losers are roaring?

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: a proper competition with a beaten side making a noise about it
the reading the setter means: roaring drunk, which is the state the forfeits leave you in

explanation.surface: A competition whose beaten players are bellowing about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Losing a round costs you another drink, so the penalty is what makes the losers loud. 'Roaring' is half of 'roaring drunk' and is the only word here doing any cryptic work.
explanation.definitionFit: A drinking game is a contest whose forfeit is a drink, so its losers finish it roaring drunk — the clue read the setter's way.

clue.text: Antagonist wrecked, seeing low times

definitions.note: 'Low times' is plural where the answer is a single mass noun; the phrase names one flat stretch of months or years rather than a set of countable occasions.

indicators.note: A wreck is what is left when a thing has been broken up, so the letters beside the word are to be built again in another order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: An opponent left in pieces and going through a bad patch.
explanation.walkthrough: A long word standing alone at the front of a clue with an instruction right behind it is nearly always the raw material. Stagnation is the economist's word for an economy that has stopped growing without actually shrinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Stagnation is a spell in which nothing moves or grows, which is what a run of low times amounts to.

clue.text: Possessive character?

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: clingy, unwilling to let anybody out of sight
the reading the setter means: a character is a mark on the page, and this is the one that marks possession

explanation.surface: Somebody described as a clingy sort of person.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, each with a human sense and a printing sense, and the clue works only when both flip at once. The mark earns its name in 'the dog's bowl'.
explanation.definitionFit: English marks possession with this one character, so among the symbols on a keyboard it is the possessive one.

clue.text: Records what judge does: hangings

blocks.note: to tape a programme is to record it
a judge tries a case, the verb for hearing it in court

explanation.surface: A note of a judge's business, hangings included.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hangings' reads as executions and means wall coverings, the woven sort that kept the draughts out of castles. Both pieces are third-person verbs, which is what keeps the surface grammatical.
explanation.definitionFit: A tapestry is a heavy woven cloth made to be hung on a wall, so 'hangings' names them by where they live.

clue.text: Cringes, losing head, wobbling - give up!

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter it begins with, and losing it drops that letter before anything else is done.
A thing wobbling will not stay where it is put, and letters that will not stay put are not to be left in the order given.

blocks.note: CRINGES without its opening C, the six letters that then get shaken up

explanation.surface: Somebody flinching and unsteady on their feet, being told to pack it in.
explanation.walkthrough: The head comes off before the shuffle starts, which is why no C turns up in the answer. 'Give up' here means handing in a post rather than being beaten, and the answer is the verb for it.
explanation.definitionFit: To resign is to give up a job or a position, the voluntary kind of stopping that 'give up' also carries.

clue.text: Household name, the PM? For the most part

indicators.note: Taking most of a thing leaves the rest behind, so the name beside it is cut short and only its front is kept.

blocks.note: Keir Starmer became Britain's prime minister in July 2024, and the question mark grants that he is only the holder of the moment

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the prime minister counts as a household name.
explanation.walkthrough: A clue pinned to whoever holds the job will date, and the question mark is the setter admitting it. The definition wants the celebrity sense of the answer, nothing to do with the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: A star is somebody famous enough that everybody knows the name, which is exactly what a household name is.

clue.text: Moves unsteadily - after second, falls

indicators.note: What comes after a thing is placed behind it, so the piece named next goes on the end of the letter already given.

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for second, the one printed on a stopwatch
a tumble is a fall, and the two match as verbs as well as nouns

explanation.surface: Somebody lurching about and going down a moment later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After second' reads as a moment's delay and is really placing a single letter. Definition and pieces are all third-person verbs, which is what lets the clue read as a sentence about one person.
explanation.definitionFit: To stumble is to walk with the feet catching and the balance going, which is moving unsteadily.

clue.text: Is tucking into gin and tonic, in summary

indicators.note: To tuck into something is to get right inside it, so the word before goes in among the letters that follow.

blocks.note: a gin and tonic is ordered at the bar as a G and T, the drink's two initials
the word is taken as it stands and set between them

explanation.surface: Someone making short work of a gin and tonic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucking into' is what you do to food and drink and is also the instruction to go inside. The initials are all a bar order leaves of the drink's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The gist of a speech is its substance boiled down to a sentence, which is what a summary gives you.

clue.text: Currently, Satanists carousing having imbibed drop of Dubonnet

indicators.note: People carousing are drinking and reeling about, and letters doing the same will not stay in the order they were given.
To imbibe is to take a thing in, so the letter that follows joins the mix being shaken rather than standing apart from it.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
the first letter — the drop off the front — of the drink's name

explanation.surface: Devil-worshippers on a spree who have had a little Dubonnet.
explanation.walkthrough: Dubonnet is a sweetened French aperitif, and 'drop of' is the standard request for the first letter of a drink. The definition is the single word at the front, fenced off by its comma.
explanation.definitionFit: As it stands means as matters are at this moment, which is what currently says of the present state of things.

clue.text: Many cigars he misplaced: pity

indicators.note: Something misplaced has ended up where it does not belong, so every letter beside the word is to be put somewhere else.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters

explanation.surface: A man who has mislaid a great many cigars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misplaced' does both jobs at once: the cigars go astray on the surface and the letters go astray underneath. Fodder split by a pronoun is the hardest sort to spot, because 'he' looks like grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: A crying shame is a turn of events bad enough to be worth lamenting, the sense of pity in 'what a pity'.

clue.text: Part of the German arthouse?

blocks.note: to be in a thing is to be part of it, as a player is in the side
die is one of the German words for 'the', the feminine and plural form

explanation.surface: Asking which bit of the German art cinema is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The German' is the article rather than the person, and that is the whole trick. The films are made away from the big studios, and the arthouse is where they get shown.
explanation.definitionFit: An indie film is one made outside the studio system, which is what 'arthouse' describes on a cinema listing.

clue.text: Mythological beast resembling Irish instrument?

blocks.note: the harp is Ireland's national emblem, stamped on its coins and on its stout
the ending -y turns a noun into an adjective meaning 'like that thing', as in chalky or bony

explanation.surface: A creature out of legend that looks rather like the Irish harp.
explanation.walkthrough: The suffix is the piece to spot: one letter, asked for by a word that looks like ordinary comparison. A harpy in Greek myth is a bird with a woman's face, sent down to snatch things away.
explanation.definitionFit: The harpy of Greek myth is a winged monster with a woman's head, so 'mythological beast' is a plain description of it.

clue.text: Close-fitting when arms raised

indicators.note: What is raised is lifted up the page, and in a down entry that means its letters are read from the bottom back to the top.

blocks.note: arms are weapons, and guns are the plainest sort

explanation.surface: A jacket that pulls tight the moment you lift your arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arms' is the body's pair on the surface and the armoury's kind underneath, and the instruction only works because the entry runs down the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Something snug sits against you with no slack left in it, which is close-fitting.

clue.text: Shy collection of actors

blocks.note: read as the verb: to shy a ball is to throw it
read as the noun: everybody named on the playbill

explanation.surface: A retiring bunch of actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shy' looks like the adjective describing the players and is the verb for throwing, the sense kept alive by the coconut shy at a British fairground. One half is a verb and the other a noun, which is how the join goes unnoticed.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast is to throw, which is what shying a stone means; and the cast of a play is everybody acting in it.

clue.text: Get in the way of somewhat dim pedestrian

indicators.note: Somewhat means only a part, so a piece of the words that follow is wanted rather than the whole of them.

blocks.note: six consecutive letters beginning one letter into the first word and stopping four letters into the second

explanation.surface: A slow-witted person out walking.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts one letter in and ends in the middle of a word, which is the easiest kind to miss when both words are this ordinary. 'Somewhat' is the standing signal that the letters are already written out for you.
explanation.definitionFit: To impede somebody is to obstruct them, standing in their way so that they cannot get on.

clue.text: 'Socialist Republic' India lies alongside, now known as, primarily ... this

definitions.text: 'Socialist Republic' India lies alongside, now known as, primarily ... this

indicators.note: What comes primarily comes first, so each word in the run gives up the letter it begins with and nothing else.

blocks.note: the quoted phrase shrunk to its two initials, the way USSR was built
India is I in the radio alphabet
the opening letter of each of the five words in turn

explanation.surface: A note on which socialist republic sits next to India and what the place goes by these days.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word does two jobs: read straight the sentence describes the country, read down the initials it spells it. The island was Ceylon until 1972, and its official name is the Democratic Socialist Republic.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the socialist republic lying off India's southern coast, called Ceylon until 1972 and known by this name ever since.

clue.text: Crazy scene accommodating first of Italian relatives

indicators.note: Somebody crazy is not in their right mind, and the letters beside the word are not to be left in their right order either.
To accommodate a guest is to find room for them indoors, so the letters just made open up and take the next one inside.

blocks.note: the five letters of SCENE in a new order
the opening letter of Italian, dropped in behind the N

explanation.surface: A chaotic house party putting up the first of the Italian relations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First of Italian relatives' reads as one phrase about which cousins turned up, and only its last word is the definition. The letter goes in after the shuffle, not before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A niece is a brother's or sister's daughter, which makes nieces relatives by the plainest reckoning there is.

clue.text: Crossword setter, we're told, ridiculous thing to behold? That makes sense

definitions.note: The definition is put as a remark rather than a noun, which is the setter's joke: it has to be read as 'that constitutes a sense'.

indicators.note: Being told a thing is hearing it, so what matters is how the word sounds and not how it is written down.

blocks.note: the setter calls himself I when he turns up in his own clue, and said aloud that is the organ
calling somebody a sight means they look a fright

explanation.surface: The setter owning up to being a ridiculous thing to look at.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's own I is the first piece and has to be heard rather than read. 'What a sight' is what British English says of anybody who looks a mess.
explanation.definitionFit: Sight is one of the five senses, so an answer that literally is a sense satisfies the idiom word for word.
